summary: Describes the conventions to be followed by those who run networks and hosts on the Internet, summarizing the unwritten oral tradition on the subject. It is one author's view and informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes responsibilities for people who manage Internet networks and hosts. It emphasizes that managers should be reachable and work with other sites to resolve problems.

subtitle: An informational account of host and network managers' responsibilities.

tldr.problem: Network and host problems can affect other sites, so the Internet depends on cooperation among the people who manage its components.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC summarizes expectations for manager contact details, operational control, postmaster mailboxes, and cooperative handling of user, host, and network problems.
tldr.outcome: It records one author's view of Internet operating conventions and explicitly does not establish an official policy or standard.

today: RFC 1173 is Informational and presents the author's view of host and network manager responsibilities. It does not specify an Internet standard or IAB policy.

sections.title: Shared Responsibilities
sections.content:
The memo says the Internet is a cooperative effort whose usefulness depends on reasonable behavior from users, hosts, and routers. People responsible for its components MUST know their responsibilities, attend to local conditions, and be accessible by Internet mail and telephone.

Local issues such as system crashes or power failures can have effects elsewhere, and diagnosing problems may require people at more than one site to cooperate.
sections.plainLanguage: Network problems can cross site boundaries. The RFC says responsible people need to be reachable and respond to reports from others.

sections.title: Network, Host, and Mail Contacts
sections.content:
Each IP network or subnet should have identified managers, with current contact information supplied to the Internet NIC or the local or regional transit network's NIC. A network manager must have system-management access or authority to isolate a misbehaving host. The RFC sets availability expectations for managers, including round-the-clock reachability for managers of transit networks and important systems.

Each Internet host needs a responsible system manager. A host that handles mail beyond its local network MUST maintain a postmaster mailbox as a contact point for mail-delivery problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Every network and host needs a responsible contact who can help fix problems. Mail-handling hosts also need a postmaster mailbox for delivery issues.

sections.title: Handling Problems and Security
sections.content:
The RFC groups network-wide problems as user-related, host-related, or network-related. It describes possible responses such as education, reconfiguration, software changes, restricting access, or escalating a network problem.

It warns managers that the Internet is not secure and says each host manager remains responsible for that host's security. It also stresses cooperation among managers when one site's users or systems cause problems for others.
sections.plainLanguage: Different problems need different responses, but managers need to communicate across sites. The memo also warns that each host manager is responsible for local security.

sections.title: Status of the Memo
sections.content: RFC 1173 describes itself as an informational summary of the author's view of the Internet's “oral tradition.” The RFC Editor's note says it was expected to provide a basis for possible future official policies, and the memo does not specify a standard or IAB policy.
sections.plainLanguage: This document records one author's view of operating conventions. It does not establish a standard or official IAB policy.
